title: Optical platform for functional longitudinal imaging of metabolite uptake in vivo
text:
Cancer metabolic reprogramming plays an essential role in tumor development resulting in differential utilization
of many essential metabolites by cancer cells compared to normal cells and has been recently recognized as a
promising therapeutic target for the improved cancer treatments. However, cancer metabolic reprogramming is
poorly understood due to the lack of tools that can quantify nutrient uptake in relevant animal models of human
cancers. Here, we propose to develop a novel optical imaging platform that would become a universal analytical
method for monitoring nutrient uptake in tumors and would help to understand metabolic vulnerabilities of many
different cancers with the overall goal to generate novel, effective treatments.

title: Co-Producing a Trauma and Substance Use Mental Health Literacy Intervention
text: This K01 Mentored Research Scientist Development Award will partner with a Community Advisory Board to co-produce and pilot a theory-guided mental health literacy intervention focused on trauma and substance use. Post-study focus groups with intervention participants will be held to elicit feedback on relevance, feasibility, acceptability, and satisfaction with the intervention to inform refinement and future dissemination efforts. The potential public health impact is large, as there are substantial disparities in mental health treatment engagement among groups with elevated risk for trauma exposure, subsequent mental health concerns (e.g., posttraumatic stress disorder, substance use), and poor outcomes from untreated mental health conditions—particularly given the myriad psychological and emotional impacts of the Covid-19 pandemic.

title: Arrhythmia mapping using electromechanical wave imaging
text:
Arrhythmias increase the risk of heart attack, cardiac arrest and stroke while atrial
fibrillation alone is expected to affect 12 million U.S. patients by 2050. The current
treatment procedures are lengthy, costly and are plagued by low to moderate success
rates. Our objective is to assess the clinical role of our ultrasound-based imaging
methodology that can better identify arrhythmic origins and focally inform on the success
of subsequent arrhythmia treatment so as to substantially improve the current success
rates and abbreviate procedure duration and/or number of procedures.

title: Changes in transient receptor potential melastatin 8 expression and function after corneal nerve regeneration
text:
This project investigates how the cold sensor transient receptor potential melastatin 8
(TRPM8) ion channel influences corneal nerve recovery and how its expression and function changes during the
healing process after injury. Correlating structural changes to functional changes will offer novel insight into why
some patients experience chronic pain, reduced sensation, and/or impaired healing after injury. The findings
from this project may guide the development of new therapies to improve outcomes for patients with nerve-
related corneal pathologies and pain.

title: Heterosynaptic mechanisms driving elevated synaptic inhibition and plasticity impairments following ischemia.
text:
Global cerebral ischemia resulting from cardiac arrest often results in cognitive and memory impairments in
survivors. This proposal will investigate changes in inhibitory synaptic transmission that contribute to synaptic
dysfunction and ultimately, memory impairments. Our long-term goal is to identify novel therapeutic targets to
improve cognitive outcomes after cardiac arrest.

title: Mechanisms of antigen-specific T cell activation in MOGAD
text:
Myelin oligodendrocyte glycoprotein antibody-associated disorder (MOGAD) is a recently described
neuroinflammatory syndrome characterized by intralesional CD4+ T cells, yet the pathogenic CD4+ T cell
specificity, T cell receptor usage, phenotype, and how these pathogenic T cells are activated are unknown.
Describing the pathogenic MOG-specific T cell receptor repertoire in humans and improving T cell and B cell-
dependent models are critical for understanding MOGAD immunopathology and advancing the goal of future
therapies. This project utilizes a complementary approach of human and mouse immunology and new
techniques in genome engineering to investigate pathogenic T cell development in MOGAD.

title: Enhancing prognosis communication for older adults in skilled nursing facilities
text:
Older adults admitted to a skilled nursing facility (SNF) for post-acute rehabilitation after a hospitalization
represent a vulnerable population at high risk for adverse events, and they would benefit from a
communication tool that provides personalized prognostic information to help guide future planning and shared
decision-making. This K76 Beeson proposal will (1) develop and compare novel machine learning-based
prognostic models to traditional regression for predicting multiple outcomes while at a SNF (hospital
readmission, transition to a nursing home for long-term care, and 6-month mortality), (2) assess prognosis
communication needs and develop and refine a SNF prognosis communication tool which contains
personalized prognostic risk estimates, anticipatory guidance for SNF care, and questions to elicit values and
preferences, and (3) pilot the prognosis communication tool in a SNF to evaluate its feasibility, acceptability,
and preliminary impact on patient-centered outcomes. The prognosis communication tool developed and pilot-
tested through this proposal will help improve clinical care for patients at a SNF by increasing prognostic
awareness, aligning expectations through enhanced communication, and facilitating shared decision-making
discussions.

title: Project 2: Translating Genomics to Practice to Overcome Disparities in Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL)
text: Investigations into the biological factors underlying differences in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL) outcomes in specific patient populations have been limited even in the largest clinicopathologic cohorts and clinical trials. A comprehensive approach that incorporates biologic contributors can overcome past limitations by defining molecular features of DLBCLs across populations; directly testing their therapeutic vulnerabilities using ancestry-specific disease models; and deploying diagnostic and treatment strategies geared for community practices.

title: Impact of Diet-Induced Dyslipidemia on Skin Inflammation Driven by Autoreactive Lipid-Specific T Cells.
text:
Hyperlipidemia, often resulting from Western dietary habits, is a major risk factor for cardiovascular disease
and is increasingly linked to autoimmune conditions. This project will investigate how high-fat diets promote
skin inflammation by activating group 1 CD1-restricted T cells that recognize self-lipids. Understanding this
connection may inform new therapies for psoriasis and other lipid-associated inflammatory diseases by
targeting this T cell subset.

title: University of Washington Interdisciplinary Center for Exposures, Diseases, Genomics & Environment
text:
The Center for Exposures, Diseases, Genomics & Environment (EDGE) fosters novel translational research on
environmental exposures associated with diseases. Using collaborative teams, advanced molecular signatures
associated with exposures, novel data sciences approaches, clinical and population scale studies, and
community engaged research, EDGE seeks to explain interactions between genetic, epigenetic and
environmental factors. The result is a better understanding of how exposures contribute to chronic and acute
diseases of public health importance, and how to prevent these effects and hence reduce the burden of
environmentally related diseases.

title: Molecular Neurobiology of Human Opioid Use Disorder
text:
The abuse of opioids including heroin is at epidemic proportions in the USA. Our research is dedicated to
expanding knowledge about molecular impairments directly in the brains of the human drug abusers to guide
the development of new targeted medications.

title: Impact of recurrent genetic alterations on SCLC subtypes and therapeutic response
text:
Current therapeutic interventions for small cell lung cancer (SCLC) are limited in scope. In this study, we propose
using mouse models with different co-genetic alteration to better understand the heterogeneity and replication
stress that hindered the treatment outcomes for SCLC patients. Furthermore, we will utilize these models to
evaluate rational drug combinations that can generate effective and durable responses for this dismal disease.

title: Core C
text:
Single-cell multi-omics study provides an unprecedented opportunity to understand immune and molecular basis
of severe asthma. We will develop bioinformatic and computational tools to analyze and integrate different types
of single-cell data. Our methods and unique multi-omics data will be immediately useful for current and future
asthma projects in a wide range of research community in pulmonary medicine.

title: Automated Planning and Robotic Delivery of Needle Biopsies under CT Image Guidance
text:
This project proposes an artificially intelligent, semi-autonomous planning and robotic approach for lung cancer
biopsy leveraging MR guidance. An AI-enabled robot planner identifies the least traumatic and safest biopsy
needle approach for a particular patient, and then, a dexterous robot inserts the needle under real-time CT
guidance. This automated method will allow patient-specific information to be incorporated into planning for
lung biopsies, enabling sensitive anatomies to be avoided, lesions to be reached faster and more accurately,
providing significant more effective screening and safety than today’s freehanded approach.

title: Lung Cancer
text: The overall goal of the Lung Cancer (LC) Program is to improve lung cancer patient survival by optimizing early detection strategies and developing novel therapeutic approaches for patients with late-stage disease, including for small cell lung cancer patients. The fact that the number of deaths attributable to lung cancer in the US has declined from 190,000 to 130,000 over the preceding decades provides reason for optimism on two fronts: substantial reductions in cigarette smoke consumption, particularly in the US, have led to a decrease in the number of lung cancer diagnoses; and five-year survival rates broke 20% for the first time for lung cancer patients, strongly suggesting that novel treatments are meaningfully impacting the disease. Despite these improvements in incidence and survival rates, these metrics compare very poorly to almost all other cancer types. Underlying these dismal statistics reside two fundamental issues. First, our ability to identify lung cancer at early states remains flawed, despite the introduction of legitimate screening practices. Second, our therapeutic strategies for patients diagnosed at an advanced stage continue to leave much to be desired. These two fundamental shortcomings must be addressed to produce a meaningful improvement in lung cancer patient outcomes. Research from the program also addresses critical deficiencies in lung cancer care available to patients residing within our catchment area. The LC Program has three specific aims to: 1) improve the efficacy of immune based therapies for lung cancer patients, 2) implement effective strategies for lung cancer screening and early detection, and 3) identify and exploit therapeutic vulnerabilities in SCLC. The program is a new program for this Cancer Center Support Grant renewal and is led by a team spanning many aspects of lung cancer research including basic, translational, population science, and clinical research in both non-small cell lung cancer small cell lung cancer, as well as clinical expertise in thoracic oncology and pulmonary medicine. The program is comprised of 34 members from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center and the University of Washington, the majority having dual appointments and bringing expertise in a diverse array of both lung cancer science and lung cancer clinical care. Members hold $9.8M in research funding, including an NCI P50 Lung SPORE. The LC program is a highly collaborative group; 19% of the 73 publications in the most recent 12-month reporting year were intraprogrammatic and 33% were interprogrammatic. Twenty-two percent were in journals with impact factors >10. Members are also actively engaged in national networks and cooperative groups.

title: SCLC Model Generation and Therapeutic Analysis
text:
High-fidelity cancer models that accurately reflect human small cell lung cancer biology play a key role
in the development of new therapeutic strategies. The Model Generation and Therapeutic Analysis Core (Core
B) for this Program will use CRISPR genome engineering technology to generate isogenic SCLC cell lines and
somatically engineered mouse models, and streamline in vivo therapeutic analysis.

title: Mass Spectrometry Shared Resource
text: Overview: Proteomics, metabolomics, and lipidomics are critically essential techniques in cancer research. The Mass Spectrometry Shared Resource (MSSR), presented as a new UCCC SR in this application, supports UCCC members by utilizing mass spectrometry technologies to characterize a wide range of molecules in cancer biology applications. Services and Expertise: The primary focus of the MSSR is to provide the equipment and staff expertise to support application of, and education in, a range of MS-based methods. The MSSR mission is supported by a highly knowledgeable staff with >80 years combined experience in analytical methods to support biomedical research. Equipment: The MSSR houses 10 mass spectrometers, enabling global and targeted analysis of simple to highly complex biological samples. Management: The MSSR is co-directed by Dr. K Hansen (THI), a biochemist and proteomics expert who leverages mass spectrometry studies to investigate the tumor microenvironment, and Dr. A D'Alessandro (MCO), a biochemist and metabolomics expert who leverages MS to study cellular reprogramming in cancer and red blood cells. MSSR managers Dr. J Reisz Haines and Dr. M Dzieciatkowska collectively have >40 years of experience in Mass Spectrometry in academia and industry. Use of Services: Since July 2016, the MSSR has supported 268 investigators, including 55 UCCC members, 42 investigators from other NCI cancer centers, 152 other academic researchers, and 19 researchers at biotech organizations. UCCC members from all four programs have used MSSR services accounting for 38% ($971K) of total revenues over the period ($2.6M) and resulting in 56 cancer-related publications. Operating Budget: In the proposed budget model, CCSG funding represents 13% of the total ($1.2M) with the remaining from user fees (72%) and institutional support (15%). Innovation and Developments: The MSSR continually innovates and expands services to address evolving user needs and new opportunities in biomolecule characterization. In the most recent funding period, the MSSR added new services (e.g., crosslinking MS, metabolic flux analysis on as few as 250 cells) and equipment (Orbitrap Fusion Lumos and an inductively coupled plasma [ICP] MS), established a library of standards to enable quantitative measurements, and rapidly implemented remote operation for all staffing to ensure uninterrupted service during the COVID-19 pandemic. Future Directions: The MSSR will continue to provide support for MS-based research by UCCC members through acquisition and deployment of cutting-edge equipment, development of new methods, and expansion of training. To remain competitive, we will: i) develop a high-throughput plasma proteomics platform, building upon our acquisition of a 4D MS system (Bruker timsTOF Pro) and ii) increase throughput capabilities with the purchase of an Orbitrap Exploris and at least one high-parameter MS system for proteomics.

title: lncRNA Function and Mechanisms during Cardiac Development and Disease
text:
Our primary research goal is to understand the function of long non-coding RNAs in the cardiovascular system.
In this project, we will examine whether the large intergenic non-coding RNA called lincRNAp21 can alleviate
pressure overload induced cardiac hypertrophy, a medical condition that is a leading cause of death worldwide
and highly relevant to the mission of the NIH. Our studies using mutant mouse models are designed to be
translated into novel therapeutic strategies to treat patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.

title: Transfusion transmitted infections and pathogen reduction technology.
text:
Transfusion transmitted infections (TTIs), such HIV, hepatitis, malaria, or an emerging infection, from a blood
transfusion pose substantilal risk. Blood donor deferral and screening are insufficient to fully protect transfusion
recipients and a proactive system such as the Mirasol pathogen reduction technology (PRT) is needed.
Combining metagenomic sequceing and samples from a clinical trial of Mirasol PRT will improve the
understanding of the risks of TTIs and potential mitigation strategies to ensure safe blood transfusions.

title: In Utero Trophoblast Transgenesis
text:
A major obstacle in understanding the role of potential mediators of placental development and analysis of
placental dysfunction has been the lack of a facile method for trophoblast gene manipulation in intact animals.
We propose to validate a novel in utero trophoblast transgenesis approach, in which lentiviral infection of
blastocysts in utero provides a rapid, trophoblast-specific, and highly efficient way to evaluate critical mediators
of placental development and pregnancy-associated disorders.
